title: Ralph Lauren Faces Backlash for Uncredited Zardozi Gown at Fashion Week
excerpt: A Spring 2027 gown shown in New York was described by the brand as having "hand-applied embellishments" — with no mention of India or zardozi. Critics say this is how global fashion erases the artisans behind the work.
body:
• A deep pink evening gown from Ralph Lauren's Spring 2027 collection has drawn backlash online after the brand's Instagram post described its intricate embroidery as generic "hand-applied embellishments" without naming India or the zardozi technique.
  • Fashion designer Prakhar Rao Singh Chandel called out the omission on Instagram, noting that Lucknow zardozi holds a Geographical Indication registration and supports around 175,000 artisans.
  • The row follows a pattern: Prada's uncredited Kolhapuri-style sandals in 2025, Ralph Lauren's jhumka-like earrings and Bandhani-inspired skirt earlier this year.
  • The brand has not issued a verified public response to the latest criticism.

A deep pink evening gown featuring intricate embroidery, shown by Ralph Lauren at New York Fashion Week, has drawn flak on social media, with users accusing the American fashion brand of failing to credit Indian craftsmanship. The controversy erupted after Ralph Lauren's official Instagram account shared images of the gown on September 12, including a close-up of its embroidery.

The caption read: "Draped with shimmering silk-viscose and scattered with hand-applied embellishments, an eveningwear gown from #RalphLaurenSpring2027 makes a cinematic statement." The post describes the fabric and embellishments in elaborate detail but does not refer to India or identify the craft used in the embroidery.

What is zardozi

The technique in question is zardozi, an elaborate embroidery tradition involving metallic threads and decorative elements. It has Persian roots at least 300 years old and flourished in India under Mughal patronage, developing distinctive regional traditions. Lucknow zardozi received a Geographical Indication registration in 2013, covering Lucknow and six surrounding districts with around 175,000 artisans working in the cluster, according to designer Prakhar Rao Singh Chandel, who drew attention to the issue in an Instagram post.

https://x.com/livemint/status/2099107794196865194

Chandel criticized the wording used by Ralph Lauren, arguing that while the brand's post gives the fabric an elaborate description, the intricate handwork has been reduced to a single reference to "embellishments." He also highlighted the final slide of the Instagram post, which features a quote from Ralph Lauren about wanting every garment to carry its own history and character. Responding to that statement, Chandel asked a pointed question.

"Whose history? Whose character?"

— Prakhar Rao Singh Chandel, fashion designer, on Ralph Lauren's zardozi-style gown

"Name it when you use it"

Chandel accused international fashion labels of repeatedly using Indian crafts without acknowledging their origins, with apologies coming only after the issue is publicly highlighted. Referring to a similar controversy involving Prada last year, he wrote: "We already know how this goes, because we watched it last year. Prada showed Kolhapuri-style sandals in Milan in June 2025, and the show notes called them leather sandals. India was named two days after the Maharashtra Chamber of Commerce wrote to their board. That is the tactic. Say nothing, take the applause, produce the credit only once somebody forces you to."

"Name it when you use it. Not when you get caught."

— Prakhar Rao Singh Chandel, fashion designer

The sentiment was echoed across the post's comments. Instagram users wrote: "Start acknowledging Indian art," "Indian embroidery inspired by Indian crafts," and "Lol literally embellishments from India. Stop stealing craft." Another wrote: "Racism towards Indians while actively stealing every part of their lifestyle, culture, and the very core of their identity is a level of audacity that needs to be studied."

A recurring pattern

The latest criticism comes amid a series of 2026 flashpoints involving Ralph Lauren and Indian-inspired fashion. Earlier this year, the brand faced online criticism over earrings resembling traditional Indian jhumkas, described in captions as "authentic vintage accessories," and a printed wrap skirt compared with Bandhani, the tie-dye craft of Gujarat and Rajasthan, priced at around $500 while handcrafted Bandhani typically sells for ₹500 to ₹5,000 in India.

Ralph Lauren is hardly alone. Prada's Kolhapuri-style sandals were labeled simply "leather sandals" until the Maharashtra Chamber of Commerce intervened, and Dior has faced criticism for a high-priced coat featuring mukaish embroidery from Lucknow without crediting the craft or its artisans.

For critics, the question is not whether designers can draw inspiration from traditional techniques. It is about recognizing the history, identity, and craftsmanship behind them — and whether heritage techniques repackaged and sold at luxury prices should name and compensate the communities that created them. As consumers grow more aware, the pressure is shifting: it is no longer enough to reference tradition in vague terms. People want to know where a design comes from, who made it possible, and whether those communities are being acknowledged.

What's next

Ralph Lauren has not issued a verified public response specifically addressing the zardozi criticism, and has not publicly described the technique as zardozi. If history is any guide, the pressure is likely to build — the Prada episode ended with the brand naming the craft after industry bodies wrote in. For now, the debate continues around a simple question: when traditional craftsmanship inspires high fashion, should the craft itself get a name and a credit?
image_caption: A close-up shows bead-and-thread embroidery on a pink Ralph Lauren gown, shown beside the gown worn on the runway. Critics identified the work as zardozi after the brand described it only as 'hand-applied embellishments.'
nri_angle: The diaspora sits at the center of this debate — Indian-American designers and consumers have been among the loudest voices demanding global brands name the crafts they borrow.
